notes: The Cognition.X companion to the SmartCiti.X New Orleans Trades Edition (the Crescent Works campus and its walkable city layer). Five tracks of port, ground, water, power and pathway — the trades as New Orleans actually works them. Control-discipline themes mirror the SmartCiti.X simulator rubrics (crane swing management, the trench's flagged utility, ordered procedure), and the honesty stance is shared verbatim: a simulator teaches control discipline and never counts as equipment certification. Facts are public-record Louisiana; transfer checks are phrased against the learner's own parish or home, and every check stays safe — observation from public ground, rated tags and paper trails, never contact with energized, suspended or moving equipment.

tracks.name: The port and the crane: cargo across the levee

themes.theme: A city that works by water
themes.description: Why New Orleans exists where it does — the river trade above it, the Gulf below it, and what a port city's work looks like from the levee.
themes.transfer_check: Find, on a real map, the port facility nearest your parish and name two things that actually move through it.

themes.description: What the operator of a wharf crane really controls — slew, trolley and hoist — and why every lift is three motions managed at once.
themes.transfer_check: Watch a real container or cargo lift, from public ground or on film, and narrate the three motions by name as they happen.

themes.theme: Rigging: the load speaks through the sling
themes.description: Slings, hitches and rated hardware — how a load's weight and balance decide the rig, and why the tag on the strap is the law of the lift.
themes.transfer_check: Examine a real ratchet strap or lifting sling, find its rated tag, and explain to someone why a frayed one is retired on the spot.

themes.description: The standard crane hand signals — one signaller, one language, no shouting over the wind.
themes.transfer_check: Learn five standard crane hand signals and demonstrate them to a partner who writes down what each one commands.

themes.description: A suspended load is a pendulum: why smooth starts and stops tame the swing, and why a hurried operator makes the load dangerous.
themes.transfer_check: Hang a small weight on a string, move your hand like a crane, and show how a slow start keeps the swing small while a jerk makes it wild.

themes.theme: The box that ate the waterfront
themes.description: Containerization — how one steel box remade longshore work, the wharves, and what a New Orleans dock job is today.
themes.transfer_check: Compare a photograph of a New Orleans wharf before containers with one today, and name three kinds of work that changed.

themes.description: Fog on the water, wind limits on the boom, and the river's stage — the conditions that stop a lift no matter the schedule.
themes.transfer_check: Look up today's Mississippi River stage at New Orleans on the public gauge and state what that number means for the docks.

themes.description: Longshore workers, operating engineers, teamsters and their halls — the crafts a single ship call brings to the wharf together.
themes.transfer_check: From one real job posting or union page for port work in Louisiana, list the craft, the hall, and one requirement for the seat.

themes.description: The intermodal chain — wharf to rail yard to truck to warehouse — and where the port's work touches your own parish.
themes.transfer_check: Pick one product in your home and trace, in writing, a plausible path it took from a ship's hold to your shelf.

themes.theme: The paper trail of a lift
themes.description: Manifests, tallies and inspection logs — why the count must match, and how paper protects both the cargo and the crew.
themes.transfer_check: Receive a real delivery of any kind, check the packing note against what arrived, and record one discrepancy or a clean count.

tracks.name: Safe ground: digging in a city below the sea

themes.description: Louisiana 811 — the one call that finds every buried line before a shovel does, and the waiting time the law demands.
themes.transfer_check: Find Louisiana 811 and write down the exact steps and the waiting period a real dig at your own address would require.

themes.description: The marking code painted on the street — red for electric, yellow for gas, blue for water — a public language anyone can read.
themes.transfer_check: Find real locate marks or flags in your neighbourhood and decode at least two colours for someone who never noticed them.

themes.theme: A trench is not a hole
themes.description: Why trench walls fail without warning, what a cubic metre of soil weighs, and why nobody enters an unprotected cut — ever.
themes.transfer_check: Weigh a small bucket of damp soil, scale the number up to a collapsed trench wall, and state the weight that would land on a worker.

themes.description: The three protections that make a trench survivable, and how the depth and the soil pick between them.
themes.transfer_check: From photographs of three real excavations, identify which protection each one uses — or flag the one using none.

themes.description: New Orleans digs into a high water table: why cuts flood from below, and what dewatering means before the real work starts.
themes.transfer_check: After a rain, note how long water stands in the lowest spot near your home, and explain what that says about digging there.

themes.theme: The line you did not expect
themes.description: Striking a buried utility — what the alarm moment is, why all work stops at once, and who must be called before anything moves again.
themes.transfer_check: Write the stop-work steps for a struck gas line as five short commands, and have someone read them back correctly.

themes.description: A trench is cut to a number, not a feeling — levels, lasers and string lines, and why half a bucket too deep is rework.
themes.transfer_check: With a string and a line level, set a level line across a real span at home and prove it with a second measurement.

themes.description: Clay, sand and fill — reading what comes out of the ground, and why the spoil pile stands back from the edge it came from.
themes.transfer_check: Sample soil from two spots near home, compare how each holds together when damp, and say which would stand in a wall longer.

themes.description: One named person inspects the trench each shift and after every rain — what that duty covers and why it cannot be shared.
themes.transfer_check: Write the checklist a trench inspection must walk through after a Louisiana thunderstorm, and defend each line.

themes.theme: Backfill and the street you leave
themes.description: Compaction in lifts, restoring the surface, and why a shortcut under the pavement becomes everyone's pothole.
themes.transfer_check: Find one patched utility cut in a real street, judge how the patch is holding, and explain what was done well or poorly.

tracks.name: Water in, water out: pumps, canals and the storm

themes.theme: A bowl between levee and lake
themes.description: The city's shape — below sea level, ringed by levees, drained by machines — and why every drop of rain must be lifted out.
themes.transfer_check: On a real elevation map, find your own ground height relative to the river and the lake, and state where your rain goes.

themes.description: The drainage pump stations and their giant screws — machinery a century old still working every storm, and the crews who run it.
themes.transfer_check: Locate the drainage pump station nearest your parish on a public map and report what area it drains and where the water lands.

themes.theme: The catch basin on your corner
themes.description: The street's first drain — where it leads, why leaves defeat it, and what a blocked basin does to the block above it.
themes.transfer_check: Find the nearest storm drain, inspect it from above without entering the street, and report whether it is clear and where its water goes.

themes.description: Outfall canals in the open air and culverts under the neutral ground — the hidden second city that carries the water away.
themes.transfer_check: Trace, on a map, the path a storm's water takes from your street to open water, naming each canal or culvert it uses.

themes.description: Hurricane season's rhythm, watch against warning, and the days-before timeline on which real preparation runs.
themes.transfer_check: Build a 72-hour countdown checklist for your own household from the public parish guidance, and post it where it can be read.

themes.description: How crews prepare equipment for a storm they will not stay to watch — fuel, elevation, tie-down, records — and why people leave on time.
themes.transfer_check: Write the shutdown-and-secure list for one real machine you have access to — a mower, a generator, a vehicle — before a named storm.

themes.theme: After the wind: reading a damaged site
themes.description: Walking a site after a storm — what to photograph, what to report, and the one rule that never bends: a downed line is untouchable.
themes.transfer_check: From photographs of storm damage, list the hazards in the order a crew must treat them, putting any wire first.

themes.description: Flood recovery labour — what wet walls become, the protective gear the work demands, and why speed matters in the first week.
themes.transfer_check: List the protective equipment a gut-out crew wears and match each item to the specific hazard it answers.

themes.description: Temporary power after a storm — and the placement rule that decides between help and tragedy: outdoors, away from windows, always.
themes.transfer_check: Find a real generator's rating plate, in person or in its manual, and mark on a sketch of your home the one safe place it could run.

themes.description: Base flood elevation, elevation certificates, and why the rebuilt house stands on piers its neighbour lacks.
themes.transfer_check: Look up whether your address sits in a mapped flood zone and report the base flood elevation the maps assign it.

tracks.name: Power back on: the grid after the wind

themes.theme: The grid you can see from the street
themes.description: Poles, transformers, service drops and the meter — the last mile of the grid, readable from your own kerb.
themes.transfer_check: From the ground and eyes only, sketch the path power takes from the nearest pole to your meter, naming each piece.

themes.theme: Why the lights go out in Louisiana
themes.description: Wind, water and trees against wires — what actually breaks in a storm, and why the same corners go dark first.
themes.transfer_check: After any outage in your parish, find the utility's public cause statement and restate it in one plain sentence.

themes.theme: The line crew's ladder of safety
themes.description: De-energize, test, ground — the fixed order a crew works through before touching anything, and why the order never varies.
themes.transfer_check: Explain the three steps and their order to someone else, and have them tell you what goes wrong if step two is skipped.

themes.description: Every downed wire is live until the utility says otherwise — the distance rule and the shuffle-step exit that keep bystanders alive.
themes.transfer_check: Teach a family member the keep-back rule and the feet-together shuffle exit, and have them repeat both back correctly.

themes.description: Hospitals and pump stations first, the biggest lines before the smallest — why restoration is a triage and your block may wait.
themes.transfer_check: Rank six fictional outage sites in restoration order and defend the ranking the way a utility would.

themes.theme: Mutual aid: crews from far away
themes.description: The convoys after a hurricane — how utilities lend crews across states, and what it takes to work a grid you have never seen.
themes.transfer_check: Find one news account of mutual-aid crews working a Louisiana storm and report where they came from and what they restored.

themes.theme: The meter and what it meters
themes.description: Reading your own meter — kilowatt-hours as a number you can watch, and what the reading says about the house behind it.
themes.transfer_check: Read your real meter twice, a day apart, and turn the difference into the cost of that day at your utility's rate.

themes.theme: Solar, batteries and the island question
themes.description: Why rooftop solar goes dark in an outage unless it can island — the safety reason lineworkers insist on it.
themes.transfer_check: Explain to someone why a solar roof alone does not power the house in a blackout, and what equipment changes that.

themes.description: Insulated tools, tested gloves and cover-up — awareness of the equipment that stands between a lineworker and the voltage.
themes.transfer_check: From a supplier's real catalogue page, identify the voltage class printed on a lineworker's glove and what the date stamp means.

themes.description: The pathway up the pole — apprenticeship years, climbing school, storm rotations — a career built one certified step at a time.
themes.transfer_check: Find one real lineworker apprenticeship serving Louisiana and write its entry requirements and its length.

tracks.name: The craft pathway: from first tool to journey card

themes.description: The hiring hall — dispatch lists, locals and the difference between looking for a job and being sent to one.
themes.transfer_check: Find one real trades local serving your parish and report what work it dispatches and how a new name gets on its list.

themes.description: Registered apprenticeship — paid hours on real work, classroom hours beside them, and a wage that steps up on schedule.
themes.transfer_check: Find one registered apprenticeship in Louisiana on the public registry and write down its entry requirements and starting wage.

themes.description: What journey-level status certifies — verified hours and verified skill — and why the card travels wherever the craft is worked.
themes.transfer_check: Interview or read an account of one journeyworker and report what their card required and where it has taken them.

themes.description: On-the-job hours and related instruction — the ledger an apprentice keeps, and why unlogged work is work that never happened.
themes.transfer_check: Keep a one-week log of your own practice at any skill, in apprentice form: date, hours, task, and who could verify it.

themes.description: What a training simulator honestly teaches — smooth inputs, swing management, ordered procedure — and the line it never crosses: no simulator hour counts as equipment certification.
themes.transfer_check: After any simulator or game that models real work, write two skills it truly built and two claims it could never certify, and say why.

themes.description: OSHA cards, craft certifications and the port's TWIC — which papers real Louisiana postings ask for, by name.
themes.transfer_check: From one real Louisiana trades posting, list every credential it names and where each one is actually obtained.

themes.description: The starter toolbox — what a first-year actually needs, the care that makes tools last, and the inventory habit that keeps them.
themes.transfer_check: Inventory the real tools in your home, mark each one's condition, and restore one neglected tool to working order.

themes.description: Stop-work authority and the near-miss report — why the newest person on site can halt it, and why writing up the close call is craft, not weakness.
themes.transfer_check: Write up one real near-miss you have witnessed anywhere, in report form: what happened, what almost happened, what changes.

themes.description: Prevailing wage, overtime and per diem — reading a trades paycheque, and the arithmetic of a storm week's hours.
themes.transfer_check: Given a real prevailing-wage rate for one Louisiana craft, compute a 50-hour storm week's gross pay with overtime, on paper.

themes.description: The projects around you — port expansions, drainage work, restoration contracts — and which crafts each one is hiring right now.
themes.transfer_check: Name two active construction, port or drainage projects in your parish and, from public sources, list the crafts working each.
